videoIdeas.title: Nobody Can Hold a Conversation Anymore
videoIdeas.hook: Half of you couldn't order a coffee without rehearsing it in your head first.
videoIdeas.rationale: My own post on people struggling to 'string a sentence together' pulled 635 views on a dead pillar for me, and Saffana's 'teach your team to write again' did 47k. There's clear appetite for the communication-skills angle — I just need to hit it harder and more often instead of once.
videoIdeas.script:
Half of you couldn't order a coffee without rehearsing it in your head first. And you think that's shyness. It's not. It's a skill you never built.

Back in the day people went outside, sat with elders, argued in the masjid car park, got humbled in real conversations. Now the most words you say out loud all day is to a self-checkout machine.

Speaking isn't a gift you're born with. It's reps. You get good at talking by talking — to strangers, to people older than you, to people who disagree with you.

Start small. Say salam first. Ask the shopkeeper a real question. Speak in the group chat's voice notes instead of hiding behind text.

The brother who can talk to anyone didn't get lucky. He just stopped being scared of sounding stupid before you did.

visuals.setting: Filmed standing in a café or on a busy high street, casual — hoodie or overshirt, natural daylight. Slightly elevated energy, talking directly to camera like you're calling out a mate.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'You've been avoiding this your whole life' over a cold shot of you standing awkwardly at a self-checkout, then cut to you talking to camera.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-sentence with no intro so it feels like you're already mid-rant
Show a phone screen full of typed messages then physically put the phone down and start speaking
Text punchline that appears only at the end: 'reps, not talent'

videoIdeas.title: We Have Fixers, We Don't Have Deciders
videoIdeas.hook: Every uncle has an opinion on your degree. Not one of them has read a single policy paper.
videoIdeas.rationale: My 'uncle and aunty have an opinion on your degree' post hit 770 views recently and is one of my strongest on-pillar leadership ideas. The framing of 'people who fix the thing vs people who decide whether it gets built' is a genuinely sharp leadership point that got buried in a long caption — it deserves to be the whole video.
videoIdeas.script:
Every uncle has an opinion on your degree. Not one of them has read a single policy paper.

Here's what nobody tells you. Our community is full of people who can fix the thing. Doctors, engineers, coders — brilliant at solving the problem in front of them. What we're short on is people who decide whether the thing should get built at all.

That's the difference between a technician and a leader. A technician answers the question. A leader chooses which question we're even asking.

We've been optimising for safe careers for two generations and wondering why we have no seat at the table where decisions get made.

You don't need everyone to become a politician. But some of you need to stop being the smartest person taking orders — and start being the one deciding what the order is.

visuals.setting: Sat down, indoors, slightly more composed and serious than the café rant — desk or bookshelf behind you, plain top. Lower, steady delivery. This is the 'older brother telling you something real' register.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'fixers vs deciders' with two columns, one filling up fast and one nearly empty, while you deliver the opening line.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: start with a blunt statement then a two-second silent pause on your face before continuing
Hold up an actual white paper / printed document as a prop on the word 'policy paper'
Split-screen text: 'answer the question' vs 'choose the question'

videoIdeas.title: Stop Being Embarrassed About Your Job
videoIdeas.hook: You're not humble. You're hiding. There's a difference.
videoIdeas.rationale: Dinoo's 'young people embarrassed about what they do for work' did nearly 12k and is exactly the punchy mindset lane that travels in our niche right now. I don't have anything in this space, and my voice would cut harder than the soft version.
videoIdeas.script:
You're not humble. You're hiding. There's a difference.

So many young Muslims are ashamed of their job. The delivery driver dodging people he knows. The lad in retail who goes quiet when the group asks 'so what do you do'. The one who skips the reunion because he's 'between things'.

Here's the thing. Where you are right now is not where you're staying — unless you let the embarrassment make your world smaller. Because that's what it does. You avoid the rooms, the people, the events that could actually pull you up, all to protect an ego that isn't feeding you anyway.

Halal income is not something to apologise for. The Prophet ﷺ tended sheep. Companions traded and laboured. Dignity was never about the title.

Work the job. Tell people what you do without flinching. And keep building quietly. The shame is costing you more than the job ever will.

visuals.setting: Walking-and-talking outdoors, or sat somewhere plain and unglamorous on purpose. Warmer, less confrontational energy than the other scripts — this one is reassurance with an edge.
visuals.visualHook: Bold on-screen text 'You're not humble. You're hiding.' held on a still frame of your face for the first two seconds before you speak.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on a mundane work setting (car, shop counter) implying relatability before you cut to camera
Text that reverses expectation: viewer expects motivation, gets called out
Whisper-to-normal volume shift on the line 'that could actually pull you up'

videoIdeas.title: 5 Things That Make You Sound Smarter Than You Are
videoIdeas.hook: You don't need a bigger vocabulary. You need to stop doing these five things.
videoIdeas.rationale: The numbered '5 X' list format is carrying Doctordaanish right now (156k on '5 careers I don't want'). I have zero list-format content. Wrapping a public-speaking lesson in a listicle structure is a proven-format play I'm currently missing entirely.
videoIdeas.script:
You don't need a bigger vocabulary. You need to stop doing these five things.

One. Filler words. Every 'like', 'basically', 'you know' is you buying time out loud. Learn to pause instead. Silence sounds like confidence. 'Errm' sounds like fear.

Two. Racing. Nervous people speed up. Slow down and people assume you know something they don't.

Three. Ending every sentence like a question. When your voice goes up at the end, you're asking permission. Land your sentences.

Four. Over-explaining. Say the thing, then stop. The person who says less with more certainty always wins the room.

Five. Apologising before you speak. 'This might be a stupid question' — you just told everyone to discount you before you opened your mouth.

None of that is talent. All of it is habit. Fix the habits.

visuals.setting: Clean, well-lit talking-head, seated. Slightly sharper look — collared shirt or neat overshirt. Punchy, confident pacing to model the advice you're giving.
visuals.visualHook: Big on-screen counter '1/5' appearing instantly with the number ticking, signalling a list so people stay to the end.
otherHookIdeas: Demonstrate the mistake badly, then correct it live (say a filler-heavy sentence, then the clean version)
On-screen text listing all 5 as tappable-looking items so people watch to 'unlock' them
Cold open on point 5 (the punchiest) then 'but let's start at one'

videoIdeas.title: Your Phone Is Making You Bad at Being Alone
videoIdeas.hook: You think you're relaxing. You're actually training your brain to panic in silence.
videoIdeas.rationale: Dinoo's dopamine/phone-addiction post did ~12k and this psychology-of-attention angle is clearly landing in the niche. It maps directly onto my mindset pillar and I have nothing on it — pure content gap.
videoIdeas.script:
You think you're relaxing. You're actually training your brain to panic in silence.

Every time there's a gap — a queue, a lift, thirty seconds of nothing — you reach for the phone. Feels harmless. But you're teaching your brain that stillness is an emergency to be escaped.

So then you sit down to read Qur'an, to study, to actually think — and you can't. Two minutes in and your hand's twitching. That's not a discipline problem. That's a wiring problem you built yourself, one scroll at a time.

Boredom isn't your enemy. Boredom is where thinking happens. It's where du'a happens, where ideas happen, where you actually hear yourself.

Start reclaiming the gaps. Stand in the queue and just stand there. Let the silence be uncomfortable. That discomfort is your focus coming back to life.

visuals.setting: Dim, calm indoor setting — evening light, quieter and more reflective delivery. Phone visible as a prop on the table. Lower energy, more 'sit down, let me tell you something'.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a close-up of a hand reaching for a phone in a moment of stillness, then freeze-frame with text 'watch what your hand just did'.
otherHookIdeas: Physically place phone face-down and slide it away on the opening line
On-screen text 'boredom is where thinking happens' held in silence for two seconds
Cold open in total silence for 2 seconds before you speak, to make the viewer feel the discomfort

videoIdeas.title: Competent and Trustworthy — In That Order Nobody Follows
videoIdeas.hook: You keep chasing influence. The Prophetic model tells you to chase the opposite first.
videoIdeas.rationale: My 'Prophetic Qualities of Leadership' post only did 508 but it's genuinely on-pillar and the Al-Qawi wal-Ameen framing is strong — it underperformed because it was a slow, quote-heavy delivery. Reworked with a blunt hook and modern examples, this is exactly the leadership content the brief wants me known for.
videoIdeas.script:
You keep chasing influence. The Prophetic model tells you to chase the opposite first.

We've got it backwards. Everyone wants the platform, the following, the voice — before they've built the character to hold it. Then they get the influence and it exposes them.

The Qur'an gives the standard in two words. Al-Qawi wal-Ameen. Strong and trustworthy. Competent and honest. Notice the order isn't 'popular and likeable'.

Strong means you can actually do the thing — you're not just loud, you're capable. Trustworthy means people can hand you responsibility and sleep at night.

That's it. That's leadership. Not the follower count. Not how well you talk. Whether you can do the job and whether you can be trusted with it.

Build those two, quietly, and the influence comes looking for you. Build it the other way round and you become another person with a mic and nothing behind it.

visuals.setting: Grounded, serious talking-head — bookshelf or plain wall, muted tones. Measured, deliberate delivery. This is the authority register, not the rant register.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen Arabic text 'الْقَوِيُّ الْأَمِينُ' with the translation 'strong + trustworthy' appearing as you say the opening line.
otherHookIdeas: Text reversal: 'influence → character' with an arrow that flips to 'character → influence'
Pause and hold eye contact after 'nothing behind it' for the close
Two-word on-screen stamp 'competent. trustworthy.' punching in one word at a time

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best-performing post by a mile — 6,138 views, 211 likes. The immediacy ('still discussing this in 2026') plus a clear stance created urgency and gave people something to agree or argue with, which is why it outran everything else you've made.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: The caption gets cut off mid-thought ('make themselves feel bett') and rambles. Your reach here is reactive-political, but that's not your stated niche. Use posts like this to earn attention, then pin a leadership/public-speaking follow-up so the new eyes have a reason to stay for what you actually want to be known for.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This 'people can't string a sentence together' post is one of your only genuinely on-pillar public-speaking pieces, and it still pulled 635 views with a relatable, blunt observation that's exactly your lane.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments and only 29 likes means it stated a problem but gave nobody a reason to respond or act. End with a challenge or a concrete first step ('say salam to a stranger this week') and ask a question in the caption to force engagement. This idea deserves a proper hook, not a wandering intro.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 'Every uncle and aunty has an opinion on your degree, none of them have read a green or white paper' is a razor-sharp, quotable line — that specificity is your voice at its best and it earned 770 views on a leadership theme.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: The strongest idea (fixers vs deciders) is buried past the fold and the caption cuts off. Lead with the sharpest line, cut the setup, and let the 'we have people who can fix the thing, few who can decide if it gets built' point be the whole video instead of the afterthought.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Clear, structured leadership content with a strong Qur'anic anchor (Al-Qawi wal-Ameen) — this is precisely the pillar the brief wants you owning, and it shows you can teach, not just react.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 508 views and 1 comment — your lowest engagement here. The delivery is quote-first and slow, so it reads like a slide rather than a hook. Open with the blunt tension ('you chase influence before character') and save the verse as the payoff, not the opener. Quote-led videos lose people in the first 3 seconds.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 24 comments on 828 views is a genuinely high comment-to-view ratio — the sectarianism angle clearly hit a nerve and got people talking, which the algorithm rewards.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: High comments but low likes (42) suggests it sparked argument more than agreement, which can pull you into refutation-page territory you've said you don't want. If you post divisive topics, steer the discussion with a pointed question so the comments build your positioning instead of just generating heat.
